section_1.title: Introduction: The Digital Ledger Problem
section_1.content: Explain the double-spending problem. Use a simple visual of 'Alice sending a digital coin' to understand why we need a decentralized way to ensure coins aren't duplicated.
section_1.example: Alice tries to send a digital image of a 10-dollar bill to Bob and Charlie simultaneously; the network must mathematically invalidate the second attempt.

section_2.title: Cryptographic Hash Functions: The Digital Fingerprint
section_2.content: Introduce SHA-256. Explain it as a one-way function: Input (any size) -> Hash Function -> Output (fixed size). Emphasize that even a 1-bit change in input completely changes the output (Avalanche Effect).
section_2.example: Visualize a 'Magic Box' where you drop a document in; it spits out a unique, scrambled alphanumeric string. If you change a single comma in the document, the string changes entirely.

section_3.title: Public-Key Cryptography: Digital Signatures
section_3.content: Prerequisite: Modular arithmetic. Explain the Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) mechanism (y² = x³ + ax + b). The private key is a large random number; the public key is the result of point multiplication on the curve.
section_3.example: A 'Robot Courier' uses a private key to sign a message. Bob uses the Robot's public key to verify that only the holder of the private key could have generated that unique signature.

section_4.title: Proof of Work: Mathematical Consensus
section_4.content: Explain how Bitcoin miners compete by finding a nonce that, when hashed with the block data, produces a hash value starting with a specific number of zeros. This is 'finding a needle in a haystack'.
section_4.example: Imagine a flock of digital squirrels racing to guess a combination lock code. The first one to click the lock (solve the hash) gets to add the next block to the tree.

section_5.title: Conclusion: Putting it Together
section_5.content: Summarize how hashing links the blocks (blockchain) and digital signatures secure the transactions, creating a tamper-proof mathematical history.
section_5.example: Think of a 'Digital LEGO Chain': Each brick is glued to the previous one by a hash, and only the person with the correct 'key' can add a new brick to the structure.
